title: FREE Lifting Plans for Fighters (Martial Arts Weight Training Programs)
summary: Part two of the martial-arts series goes through NH's free purist and hybrid lifting templates for boxing/savate, BJJ/aikido, wrestling/sambo, MMA/vale tudo, karate/kung fu, judo/sumo, muay thai/kickboxing and systema/krav maga, explaining each exercise choice. He covers recovery, scheduling, carryover through joint angles, injury prevention and reps in reserve, and stresses that the programs are flexible bases to modify.
claims: His fighter programs are final versions but meant to be modified; once you understand the spirit and purpose of a program, any change in line with it makes sense
When programming for fighters he considers recovery between muscle hits and practice, scheduling, cycles such as mesocycles, priorities, injury prevention, specificity and carryover
Fighters should not run the same program year-round as bodybuilders can; adjust volume and intensity depending on how close a competition is
For a fighter muscle building is a sub-priority; the number one priority is becoming a better fighter
Some exercises are chosen for injury prevention because they build resilience in positions the sport puts you in; the programs include no stretching
Never load a kick, punch, takedown or choke; instead pick lifts that reproduce joint angles found in the sport
Boxing Day A opens with dips or weighted push-ups 3x6-8 as the main press, then seal or incline DB rows 4x8-12 with landmine twists, to build explosive upper-body power
Punching power starts at the floor, so boxers still need leg press, hack squats or squats to avoid imbalances
Hang clean pulls are easy to learn, low impact, need little mobility, don't wreck recovery, teach exploding from the floor and build calves and traps
Hang power cleans or landmine thrusters teach gathering energy by dipping and exploding up; weighted rotations are probably overkill since rotation is trained in skill work
His programs are minimal, so neck or calf work can be moved to another day; the more exercises you can recover from, the faster the results
Good mornings may suit in-fighters (lifting the opponent's body with the torso) and deficit deadlifts out-boxers, but both are hip hinges so preference is fine
Boxers need endurance shoulders to keep the guard up when fatigued, so overhead pressing uses longer sets of 6-12
Split-stance landmine RDLs mirror the bladed boxing stance and build hamstrings and explosiveness
Grip work was added to the boxing program after commenters pointed out its importance for punching
Boxing conditioning: 3-5 dashes of 3 minutes, matching round length, at the fastest pace you can hold, progressing by covering more distance
Calf raises to AMRAP follow the dashes since boxers already stress calves with jump rope; the extra hypertrophy work cannot hurt
Diamond push-ups to AMRAP will give heavy shoulder DOMS but help shoulder mobility without risk of injury
The real difference between purist and hybrid is that hybrids can repeat the days 3-4 times a week, piling up extra tonnage
For BJJ, barbell rows or good mornings 4x8-12 force a bent-over compromised position that demands core rigidity and hip control, as on the mat
He prefers dips or weighted push-ups over bench press for BJJ because moving through space suits the sport, but bench is fine if you like it
Training a press builds muscle usable beyond pressing, such as rotating an opponent: carryover is weaker but muscle is muscle
Towel holds: loop a towel, belt or gi through a weight and hold it with extended arms for 15 seconds to build static grappling grip
GHRs or hyperextensions train the posterior chain without leg drive from the ground, useful when an opponent takes away your base
Turkish get-ups train balance, core and thoracic spine rigidity for grapplers
Any pull from the floor (conventional, trap bar or Jefferson deadlift) for 1-3 sets of 5 is a staple for martial artists
Single-leg hip thrusts suit BJJ because in positions like side control one leg is often pinned and you can only drive with one glute
Even in pull-dominant sports keep training presses for the antagonist muscles, as long as pulling volume is not sacrificed
Russian twists suit BJJ because you must rotate the torso while sitting or on your back
Rope climbing is the supreme conditioning exercise for grapplers; substitutes are sled pulls, pull-ups, lat pulldowns or dead hangs
Conditioning sessions should take 30-40 minutes, alternating intense pockets with plenty of rest, not long runs, because a BJJ match is intense
Captains of Crush grippers appear throughout the programs as a grip reminder; they can be done anywhere, or dropped if they interfere with practice
A subscriber pointed out his wrestling program had too much pushing; he agreed it had relied on a meathead stereotype and shifted it toward pulling
Zercher or SSB squats push the torso forward like an opponent pulling or pushing you and recruit the upper back, unlike orthodox back squats
Pendlay rows or lat pulldowns follow squats for wrestlers; if too fatigued to stay rigid, do cable rows instead
Staggered-stance RDLs are specific because wrestlers fight from a staggered stance
Every program includes at least one direct ab isolation exercise, even the purist ones
Wrestlers already do neck bridges, so he uses neck isolation that is less taxing and less risky
Every exercise he programs for fighters either aids injury prevention or is neutral to recovery and practice
Hang clean pulls mimic the up-and-down movement of a takedown and build traps and explosiveness
Farmer's walks help handle a wrestler's pinning pressure and build traps, grip and upper back; they pair well with kettlebell swings
For MMA he uses double-leg hip thrusts because being mounted means bridging with both legs to escape ground and pound; glute bridges are a more specific option
Medicine ball slams using hip and core rotation are more specific than decline sit-ups; ab, neck and forearm work can be moved to other days
He prefers trap bar or Jefferson deadlifts for fighters: less technical, the load sits under you, less lower-back torque and a more upright torso; sumo is for sumo specialists or very tall men
Landmine press is often called more MMA-specific, while dumbbell overhead press may be better for shoulder endurance; choose by preference
Landmine twists are among the best ab exercises for MMA because rotating the hips and core and catching the weight replicates a punch
MMA conditioning uses 5-minute dashes at top pace matching round length, or sled drags if you prioritise hypertrophy
Karate and kung fu programs emphasise pressing because projecting the shoulder matters for strikers; neutral, reverse or Swiss-bar bench grips are fine
Bruce Lee reportedly hurt his back doing good mornings with 135 lb; keep reps in reserve, e.g. stop at 10 when you could do 12
On hang pulls go light: on a hang clean pull the bar should reach at least the navel, and you should finish in a straight line on your toes
Grapplers need to move the opponent's body while preventing theirs from being moved (keeping the guard closed); strikers need explosive extension into the opponent's space
The one-arm DB press for karate is a slightly gimmicky nod to punching with one arm at a time
Pullovers expand the rib cage and develop the lats used in rotation
Sprints of 10x10 m develop short, explosive intensity for strikers
Reviewing it live, he noticed the karate program had zero knee-flexion work and added squat and Bulgarian split squat options
For judo and sumo avoid pure knee-flexion lifts like front squats; pick squats with forward lean, because the posterior chain and hip hinge are king in every martial art
Neutral-grip presses match how you grip in judo and sumo
Choose chin-ups over pull-ups because the programs have no direct biceps work, and biceps matter for grappling and injury prevention
Muay thai and kickboxing involve more strike volume than karate, so the lower body is trained for endurance legs and hips; getting flat-footed is dangerous
Croc rows are staggered-stance dumbbell rows pulled like starting a lawnmower, excellent for grip and upper back
Every program includes weighted chin-ups because they apply to every combat sport; do not skip them
Systema and krav maga programs are well-rounded because self-defence practitioners are less specialised
Bear crawls are great but rarely programmed because he finds them too taxing and redundant
Conditioning days always combine cardio, thoracic extension, abs, posterior chain and carries or bodyweight pulls, with a hypertrophy twist
Any movement grows the muscles it uses, so rope work also grows forearms and upper back
